title: Course Schedule II (Topological Sort)
description: Kahn's algorithm: BFS on nodes with in-degree 0, peeling them off the DAG. Returns a valid topological order, or [] on cycle. O(V+E).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: same setup as Course Schedule — `numCourses` and a list of `[a, b]` pairs meaning b is a prerequisite of a — but now instead of returning a boolean, I return an actual valid topological order (any one), or `[]` if a cycle makes it impossible."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Multiple valid orders — I can return ANY one, right? Tests typically accept any valid topo sort.
• Edge direction — `[a, b]` means b before a → edge b → a, same as Course Schedule I?
• Empty prerequisites — return `[0, 1, …, n-1]`? (Any permutation is valid; the natural order falls out.)
• Single course — return `[0]`.
• Cycle — return `[]` (empty array), not null or false.
sections.why: The 'any valid order' question is worth confirming explicitly — some judges accept multiple correct outputs, some pin a specific one (usually whichever Kahn's emits with FIFO queue ordering). For the natural-order question on empty prereqs: Kahn's will seed the queue with `[0, 1, …, n-1]` in iteration order, so the output is the natural order — but if the interviewer wanted lexicographically smallest among all valid orders, you'd need a min-heap instead of a queue. Asking signals you know the variant exists.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious approach before optimizing.
sections.say:
"The brute force is to enumerate every permutation of 0..n-1, and for each one check whether every prerequisite is satisfied — every `[a, b]` must have b's position less than a's position. That's O(n! · m) where m is the number of prereqs. Even for n=10 that's 3.6 million orderings to check; past n=15 it's effectively impossible.

The fix is the same as Course Schedule I: this is topological sort. If the directed graph (edges b → a for each `[a, b]`) is acyclic, a valid order exists and Kahn's BFS produces one in O(V + E); if there's a cycle, no order works and we return `[]`."
sections.why: Same as Course Schedule I — naming the n!-permutations brute force motivates the leap to graph theory: 'I don't need to try orderings; I need to derive one constructively from the dependency structure.' Calling it out also distinguishes this problem from constraint-satisfaction problems where brute force is actually the answer (e.g., when there are non-linear constraints that don't reduce to topological sort).

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to Kahn's algorithm specifically?
sections.say:
"'Find an order consistent with directed dependencies' is the topological-sort signature, and Kahn's algorithm is the cleanest way to produce one explicitly. The algorithm: build an adjacency list AND an indegree array from the edges. Seed a queue with every node whose indegree is 0 (no prereqs — these are 'roots'). Then BFS — pop a node, append it to the result order, and for each of its outgoing neighbors decrement their indegree; if any drops to 0, enqueue it (it just became a new root). When the queue drains, if you emitted all V nodes, return the order; if fewer than V, the unemitted ones form a cycle and you return `[]`.

The key insight versus Course Schedule I: in Schedule I we only counted; here we collect into an `order` array. That's a one-line difference — Kahn's already does the topological sort internally, we just have to record it.

Alternative: DFS with 3-color marking, where you append nodes to the order in post-order (after recursing into all neighbors), then reverse at the end. Detect cycles via the 'gray means on current path' check. Both algorithms are O(V + E); Kahn's is cleaner here because we don't have to reverse the output and there's no recursion stack risk."
sections.why: Naming the algorithm AND the difference from Schedule I AND the DFS alternative is what makes this conversation feel earned. 'Use Kahn's' is the trigger; 'use Kahn's because Schedule II needs the order explicitly and Kahn's collects it inline, vs. DFS which needs a reverse-postorder collection' is the derivation. Interviewers grade on the second. The 3-color DFS mention is the senior insight — it's the alternative they'll ask about, and being ready with 'either works; here's why I'm picking Kahn's' is the right level of preparedness.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a diamond DAG (multiple roots converging), a tight cycle (cycle detection via short-emission), and a linear chain (sanity check).

examples.note: Diamond DAG — 0 unlocks both 1 and 2, both feed into 3, then chain to 5. Confirms multi-out-edge decrement.
examples.trace:
build: adj[0]=[1,2], adj[1]=[3], adj[2]=[3], adj[3]=[4], adj[4]=[5]
indeg=[0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1]
seed: only indeg[0]=0 → queue=[0]
pop 0 → order=[0]; --indeg[1]=0 → enqueue 1; --indeg[2]=0 → enqueue 2 → queue=[1,2]
pop 1 → order=[0,1]; --indeg[3]=1 (NOT zero)
pop 2 → order=[0,1,2]; --indeg[3]=0 → enqueue 3 → queue=[3]
pop 3 → order=[0,1,2,3]; --indeg[4]=0 → enqueue 4
pop 4 → order=[0,1,2,3,4]; --indeg[5]=0 → enqueue 5
pop 5 → order=[0,1,2,3,4,5]
queue empty, order.length===6 → return [0,1,2,3,4,5]

examples.note: Tight cycle — both indegrees start at 1, queue never seeds, while-loop never executes.
examples.trace:
build: adj[0]=[1], adj[1]=[0], indeg=[1, 1]
seed loop: neither node has indeg=0 → queue=[]
while loop never executes → order=[]
order.length(0) !== numCourses(2) → return []

examples.note: Linear chain 0→1→2 — sanity check that single-root chains emit in order.
examples.trace:
build: adj[0]=[1], adj[1]=[2], indeg=[0, 1, 1]
seed: indeg[0]=0 → queue=[0]
pop 0 → order=[0]; --indeg[1]=0 → enqueue 1
pop 1 → order=[0,1]; --indeg[2]=0 → enqueue 2
pop 2 → order=[0,1,2]
queue empty, order.length===3 → return [0,1,2]

sections.why: Tracing surfaces two things that the boolean version (Schedule I) hides. (1) The diamond case shows the FIFO queue ordering directly impacts which topo order you emit — 1 and 2 are both available after 0, and the queue takes 1 first then 2. With a stack (LIFO) you'd get a different valid order; with a min-heap you'd get the lexicographically smallest. (2) The cycle case shows that returning `[]` is structural: order.length < numCourses is the exact condition for 'unreachable nodes exist', and those unreachable nodes are the cycle. Worth tracing once to internalize.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty prerequisites — every indegree is 0, every node seeds the queue, output is `[0, 1, …, n-1]`. ✓
• Single course `numCourses=1, prereqs=[]` — queue=[0], pop, order=[0], return [0].
• Self-loop `[[1,1]]` — `indeg[1]=1`, never enqueued; order is short → return [].
• Duplicate edges `[[1,0],[1,0]]` — `indeg[1]=2`; when 0 is popped, decrement twice (adj[0]=[1,1]). Still correct, just inflated work.
• Disconnected components — multiple zero-indegree roots seed simultaneously. Each component's order interleaves in the output based on FIFO. The interviewer might want grouped output (component-at-a-time), in which case you'd need to detect component boundaries.
• Very large input — `queue.shift()` is O(n) per call in JS arrays, which makes the loop O(V²). For interview correctness it's fine; for production use a head-index or proper deque.
• Multiple valid orders — Kahn's emits one specific order based on FIFO discipline; if the judge expects a specific tiebreak (e.g. lexicographic smallest), use a priority queue instead."
sections.why: The 'multiple valid orders → priority queue if you need a specific tiebreak' insight is the senior call-out — most candidates don't realize Kahn's order isn't unique. The disconnected-components observation is the subtle one: outputs interleave when multiple roots are available, which is correct topologically but might surprise an interviewer expecting per-component grouping. The `queue.shift()` perf concern is the same JS-specific note from Schedule I — same fix (head index).

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(V + E) where V = numCourses and E = prerequisites.length. Build is O(V + E). The BFS pops each node exactly once (V) and decrements each edge exactly once (E) across the whole loop. The output array's length is at most V.

Space is O(V + E) — adjacency list dominates at O(E), indegree and queue and order each at O(V).

If you wanted to extend to 'find the topological order with the smallest-lexicographic ties' (LeetCode 269 Alien Dictionary variant), swap the FIFO queue for a min-heap — pop the smallest available zero-indegree node each step. Same algorithm, O((V+E) log V) instead of O(V+E).

If you wanted to detect cycles AND identify exactly which nodes are in the cycle, the remainder after Kahn's drains (`indeg[i] > 0` for any i) is the union of all nodes on a cycle. That's a useful debug surface.

Same template — build adj + indegree, BFS the zero-indegree frontier — shows up in Alien Dictionary, Sequence Reconstruction, Minimum Height Trees (which uses Kahn's BFS from leaves inward!), and Parallel Courses (where you count BFS layers instead of nodes)."
sections.why: The V + E argument is textbook; same defense as Schedule I. The priority-queue extension is the obvious 'what if tiebreaks matter?' follow-up. The 'remainder identifies the cycle nodes' insight is the killer debug observation — it explains why Kahn's is preferred over DFS for cycle-finding too, because you get the cycle membership for free. The Minimum Height Trees connection is the cross-reference that proves you see Kahn's as a frontier-peeling template, not 'the algorithm for course problems' — it solves a totally different-looking problem (finding tree centroids) with the same shape, run from leaves inward.

walkthrough.intro: Step through Kahn's BFS — same skeleton as Course Schedule, but this time we collect the order. Watch each peeled node land in the order array; if a cycle traps the rest, the final check falls back to [].
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter findOrder — numCourses=${numCourses}, prerequisites=${JSON.stringify(prerequisites)}`, state: { numCourses, prerequisites } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init empty adj + indeg=[0,...,0]', state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), indeg: [...indeg] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `edge ${b} -> ${a} (b is prereq of a); indeg[${a}]=${indeg[a]}`, state: { adj: adj.map(g => [...g]), indeg: [...indeg] } };
yield { line: 12, label: `seed queue with ${i} (no prereqs)`, state: { adj: adj.map(g => [...g]), indeg: [...indeg], queue: [...queue] } };
yield { line: 13, label: `seeding done — queue=[${queue.join(',')}], order=[]`, state: { adj: adj.map(g => [...g]), indeg: [...indeg], queue: [...queue], order: [...order] } };
yield { line: 16, label: `pop ${u} — order=[${order.join(',')}]`, state: { adj: adj.map(g => [...g]), indeg: [...indeg], queue: [...queue], order: [...order], current: u } };
yield { line: 19, label: `--indeg[${v}]: ${before} → ${indeg[v]}`, state: { adj: adj.map(g => [...g]), indeg: [...indeg], queue: [...queue], order: [...order], current: u, neighbor: v } };
yield { line: 19, label: `${v} hit 0 — enqueue (becomes a new root)`, state: { adj: adj.map(g => [...g]), indeg: [...indeg], queue: [...queue], order: [...order] } };

yield { line: 23, label: `queue empty — order.length=${order.length}, numCourses=${numCourses} → return ${JSON.stringify(result)}`, state: { order: [...order], numCourses, returns: JSON.stringify(result) } };

notes: Edge direction matters: `[a, b]` means b is a prerequisite of a, so add edge b -> a and increment indeg[a].
Seed the queue with every node whose in-degree starts at 0; otherwise the BFS never begins.
If the final `order.length` is less than V, a cycle absorbed the missing nodes — return [] per spec.

alternates.label: DFS post-order with 3-color cycle detection
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer asks for the recursive/DFS variant, or when the graph is sparse and you'd rather avoid building an indegree array. Detects cycles via WHITE/GRAY/BLACK coloring: GRAY means 'on the current DFS path,' so re-entering a GRAY node is a back-edge = cycle. The topological order falls out of reverse post-order — you push each node AFTER all its descendants are finished.
notes: Three colors are the key: WHITE = untouched, GRAY = currently on the DFS stack, BLACK = fully processed. Hitting a GRAY node mid-DFS is the back-edge that proves a cycle exists.

Push each node AFTER recursing into all its descendants (post-order), then reverse the final array — a node's dependencies finish (and get pushed) before the node itself, so reversing puts prereqs first.
Output ordering will differ from Kahn's — DFS naturally produces a depth-first topo order, while Kahn's gives a breadth-first one. Both are valid; check whether the judge accepts any valid topo sort.

questions.q: What does Kahn's algorithm use as its frontier?
options: Nodes ordered by descending out-degree to drain the most dependents first
questions.explain: The queue holds only nodes with `indeg === 0` — every prerequisite already emitted — and a node joins the frontier the instant `--indeg[v]` hits 0.

options: A node's in-degree decrements below 0, signaling that a back-edge was traversed
The queue becomes empty before all V nodes are emitted
Two distinct enqueued nodes share an out-edge to the same successor
BFS revisits a node that's already in the emitted `order` array
questions.explain: Nodes inside a cycle keep each other's indegree above 0 forever, so they never enqueue; `order.length === numCourses` is the test, and a short order returns []. No indegree ever goes negative — each edge decrements exactly once.

questions.q: For `prerequisites = [[a, b]]`, the edge direction is:
options: Both a -> b and b -> a (the pair encodes a mutual dependency)
a -> b for indegree bookkeeping, but b -> a in the adjacency list
questions.explain: b is the prerequisite, so the canonical writes `adj[b].push(a)` and `indeg[a]++` — the edge points from the prereq toward the course it unlocks, and both structures use that same direction.

The build pass costs O(V + E); afterwards each node is popped from the queue once and each `adj` entry is decremented once, so no node or edge is revisited. The log factor would only appear if the queue were swapped for a min-heap to break ties lexicographically.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the edge construction and the cycle check.

blanks.hint: edge ends at the dependent course

L3.prompt: Write `findOrder(numCourses, prerequisites)` returning any valid topological order, or [] if a cycle exists. Use Kahn's BFS. Log results for a valid 4-course DAG and a 2-course cycle.
hints: Build adj-list from b -> a and tally indeg[a] for each [a, b] pair.
Seed a queue with every node whose in-degree is 0; pop, emit, then decrement neighbors.
If fewer than `numCourses` nodes are emitted, a cycle exists — return [].
